name: Castor oil on brows/lashes
lead: Brushing castor oil onto eyebrows and eyelashes is a home practice that people use hoping to get fuller, longer-looking brows and lashes. Fuller brows and lashes frame the eyes, and in looksmaxxing discussion lash and brow density feeds into how the eye area reads, including the look of canthal tilt. Castor oil is pressed from castor beans and is made up mostly of triglycerides, with ricinoleic acid making up most of its fatty acids.[1]

Users typically apply a small amount along the lash line or brow, often with a cotton swab or spoolie. Online descriptions note that the oil is also a conditioner: it coats the hair and can leave lashes looking glossier, and some users describe lashes looking healthier rather than thicker.[2] On looksmax.org it is a frequent first suggestion for brows shaved or over-tweezed by accident, where members say the hair returns in a few weeks.[3]

No published clinical trial has tested castor oil for brow or lash growth. Healthline's explainer describes the claims as anecdotal and notes that a small 2021 randomized trial found castor oil eased eyelid-inflammation symptoms in blepharitis, which is a different outcome.[2] Lash length is largely genetic, and lashes pulled out take roughly seven to eight weeks to regrow.[4]

angle.text: Users apply it to make brows and lashes look thicker, darker-looking and glossier. The visible conditioning effect is immediate; claims of added density or length rest on anecdotes.

paras: Castor oil is a pale, viscous vegetable oil with laxative, skin-care and industrial uses.[1] Two forms are sold for beauty use: cold-pressed (clear) and Jamaican black (dark brown), which Healthline describes as sharing the same properties.[2]
Typical online routines apply a small amount to clean, makeup-free lashes or brows in the evening and wash it off in the morning.[2]

Proponents point to ricinoleic acid and the oil's moisturizing feel. Healthline notes that ricinoleic acid has been discussed as possibly inhibiting prostaglandin D2, a molecule linked to male-pattern baldness, but says this is an unconfirmed possible scalp-hair mechanism and has not been shown to affect eyelashes.[2]

For context, prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost and bimatoprost are known to lengthen and thicken lashes; latanoprost, a glaucoma drug, was reported to increase lash thickness, length and pigmentation.[5] Latisse (bimatoprost) was the first FDA-approved lash-growth drug, introduced in 2009, and its maker reports noticeable growth within 16 weeks.[4] These are separate prescription products, not castor oil.

Lashes have a short growth (anagen) phase compared with scalp hair, which limits how long they grow.[6] Wikipedia reports that upper lashes typically measure 7 to 8 mm, that length is almost entirely determined by genetics, and that the number of follicles is fixed before birth.[4] Plucked lashes take about seven to eight weeks to regrow, and constant pulling can cause permanent damage.[4]

Castor oil is generally described as low in toxicity when used topically. Wikipedia notes the seeds contain ricin, which heat during extraction deactivates, and an allergen that is absent from the oil.[1] Healthline reports allergic reactions are possible and that product labels and guidance advise patch testing, keeping oil out of the eyes, and checking that a product is pure castor oil rather than a blend.[2]

Looksmax.org members discuss brows and lashes as part of the eye area, and threads range from lash lifts and tints to growth products.[7] In a thread asking whether castor oil for eyebrow growth is legitimate, one member answered yes and another said shaved brows return in two to four weeks, with tweezed ones taking longer.[3] Other threads compare castor oil with minoxidil and other approaches for lashes and brows.[8]
No studies found on castor oil for eyebrow or eyelash growth. A small 2021 randomized trial described by Healthline examined castor oil for blepharitis symptoms, not lash growth.[2]

timeline.event: Bimatoprost solution (Latisse) becomes the first FDA-approved drug for eyelash growth.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, castor oil is a common first suggestion for regrowing or thickening brows and lashes.[3][8]

claims.claim: Castor oil regrows shaved or thinned brows.
claims.believers: Forum users in an eyebrow-growth thread say it works and that shaved brows return in two to four weeks, longer if tweezed.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing castor oil for brow or lash growth.[2] Wikipedia notes plucked lashes regrow in roughly seven to eight weeks on their own.[4]

claims.claim: Castor oil makes lashes look healthier even if not longer.
claims.believers: Some users say that after about a month their lashes looked glossier and healthier, though not thicker.[2][3]
claims.experts: Healthline describes castor oil as a common hydrating ingredient and its growth claims as anecdotal.[2]

claims.claim: Minoxidil or prescription analogs work better than oils for lashes.
claims.believers: Members of looksmax.org compare minoxidil and oils for lashes and brows in several threads.[8]
claims.experts: Prostaglandin analogs are documented to lengthen lashes.[5][4]

card.summary: Folk remedy of brushing castor oil on brows and lashes for thickness; popular online, untested in trials.
card.note: No trials identified; keep oil out of the eyes.

quick.overview:
Castor oil is a thick plant oil that many people brush onto brows and lashes hoping for thicker hair.

Forum users report both positive and underwhelming results.
quick.mechanism: Proponents attribute effects to ricinoleic acid and conditioning; no study has tested this for brows or lashes.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally described as low risk, but eye-area products can irritate.
